issues.legal_issue: A later failure to perform a contractual promise does not constitute cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intent existed when the promise was made.
material_facts: The complaint concerned a land sale and alleged that the sellers had made assurances about the division and ownership of the land and concealed a pending partition suit.

The complaint did not allege, expressly or by implication, that the sellers intentionally concealed the suit or otherwise acted dishonestly at the start of negotiations to induce the buyer to part with property.
The sellers later failed to receive the full sale consideration, including because cheques issued for the balance were dishonoured.
issues.conclusion: The allegations did not make out the essential dishonest or fraudulent intention at the time of inducement required for cheating; later non-performance alone could not establish that intention.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 415 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, cheating requires deception and, for inducing delivery of property, fraudulent or dishonest inducement. The distinction between a contractual breach and cheating turns on the accused’s intention when the inducement was made; subsequent conduct may be considered but is not by itself the test, and later failure to keep a promise does not permit an inference of dishonest intention at the outset. The Court also treated the related allegations under Sections 418 and 423 as lacking the necessary basis in this case.

predicates.contractual_transaction: The allegations arise from a transaction in which one person agreed to transfer property to another for consideration.
predicates.initial_dishonest_intent_not_alleged: The complaint does not allege that the promisor had a dishonest or fraudulent intention when making the promise or inducement.

issues.definition: When a property transaction is contractual and the complaint does not allege dishonest intent at the time of inducement, the facts do not make out cheating.

issues.legal_issue: A criminal complaint must be quashed when, even accepting its allegations as true, it does not make out the charged offences.
material_facts: The buyer filed a criminal complaint alleging cheating-related offences, dishonest execution of a transfer deed, forgery, intentional insult, and criminal conspiracy in connection with the land sale.
The complaint did not allege that the sellers intentionally concealed the pending suit to induce the buyer to part with property.
The complaint contained no basic allegations making out the alleged forgery, intentional insult, or conspiracy offences.
The High Court declined to quash the complaint, and the sellers appealed.
issues.conclusion: The complaint and the proceeding based on it were quashed, and the appeals were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a criminal proceeding may be quashed where the allegations, taken at face value and accepted in their entirety, do not prima facie constitute an offence. This is the first illustrative category in State of Haryana v. Bhajan Lal; the power must be exercised sparingly and with circumspection. The Court noted that the principles in Bhajan Lal had been followed in Rupan Deol Bajaj v. Kanwar Pal Singh Gill, Rajesh Bajaj v. State (NCT of Delhi), State of Kerala v. O.C. Kuttan, P.S. Rajya v. State of Bihar, and State of Orissa v. Bansidhar Singh.

rule.if: criminal_quashing_appeal and allegations_taken_as_true and initial_dishonest_intent_not_alleged and basic_allegations_for_other_offences_absent

predicates.criminal_quashing_appeal: The matter is an appeal concerning refusal to quash a criminal complaint or proceeding.
predicates.allegations_taken_as_true: The complaint’s allegations are considered at face value and accepted as true in their entirety.
predicates.initial_dishonest_intent_not_alleged: The complaint does not allege that the accused acted dishonestly at the time of the alleged inducement.
predicates.basic_allegations_for_other_offences_abs: The complaint does not contain basic factual allegations supporting the other charged offences.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns quashing a criminal proceeding and the accepted allegations omit both the required initial dishonest intent and basic facts for the other charges, the proceeding is quashed.
